| [NOTE-015](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-015.md) v2 | Periodic vehicle routing and facility location for waste collection | The paper couples bin-capacity choice with weekly periodic capacitated routing (Sunday off, cyclic). Service time depends on the chosen bin combination, which gives an MIQP; a Glover linearisation turns it into a MILP. It solves both with Gurobi 10 for 8 h, and also with a binary-mask + permutation GA (CX 0.8, EM 0.05, pop 100, 10,000 generations). On five 12-point instances Gurobi stops at 26–32% optimality gaps. The best-of-30 GA overall cost is on average −0.08% vs the MILP incumbent and +1.70% vs the MIQP incumbent; the GA mean or median is +3.75% and +5.61%. The GA routes better (−5.75% and −5.74% routing cost) but buys much more bin capacity (+19.88% and +22.59%). On 40–163-point Bahía Blanca instances the GA returns feasible solutions in 0.72–5.58 h per run, with no bound to compare against. | Read |

| [NOTE-889](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-889.md) | Gupta — Selection of views to materialize in a data warehouse | Gupta states view selection on general AND-OR view graphs as minimizing frequency-weighted query cost plus update-frequency-weighted maintenance cost under a space budget. He proves greedy guarantees of 1 − 1/e (about 63%) of the optimal benefit, with the budget overrun by one view or up to double, but almost all of them assume no updates. Maintenance cost enters exactly one theorem: AND view graphs (each view has one way of being computed) in which every view is queried more often than it is updated. For OR view graphs, which include Harinarayan, Rajaraman and Ullman's data cube, the paper sets update costs aside outright, so it does not add upkeep to that problem. Maintenance is an abstract per-update charge for keeping a view consistent. Nothing prices building a view, tolerated staleness or deferred refresh, and there are no experiments. | Read |
| [NOTE-890](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-890.md) | Gupta & Mumick — Selection of views to materialize under a maintenance cost constraint | Gupta and Mumick choose views to materialize so as to minimize frequency-weighted query cost subject to a cap S on total maintenance time, the sum over chosen views of update frequency times a per-update maintenance cost that depends on which other views are stored. Because storing one view can make another cheaper to maintain, benefit per unit of maintenance is not monotone and the single-view greedy of earlier work can be arbitrarily bad. For OR view graphs (each view computed from one other, as in data cubes) a greedy that adds whole "inverted tree sets" gets at least 1 − 1/e (63%) of the benefit of an optimal solution that may use as much maintenance as the greedy did, the greedy using up to 2S, assuming no inverted-tree piece of the optimum alone exceeds S (Theorem 1, unproved here); without that assumption it gets half the optimum's benefit per unit of maintenance (Theorem 2). Each greedy stage enumerates exponentially many sets in general; for general AND-OR graphs there is only an exact A* search with exponential worst case. Upkeep is a budget, not a term traded against query savings; build cost, storage and staleness are not modelled, and the experiments are on random graphs of 10 to 25 nodes. | Read |
| [NOTE-895](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-895.md) | Harinarayan, Rajaraman & Ullman — Implementing data cubes efficiently | Treats a data cube's group-by queries as a lattice in which a query can be answered from any stored ancestor, prices a query at the number of rows of the smallest materialized ancestor, and chooses which views to precompute. Choosing k views to maximize the total reduction in query cost (the "benefit") is NP-complete; a greedy rule that adds the view of largest marginal benefit gets at least 1 − ((k−1)/k)^k ≥ (e−1)/e ≈ 63% of the optimal benefit, a bound that is tight, holds unchanged with query-frequency weights, and weakens to 0.63 − f under a space budget when no view takes more than a fraction f of it. The cost of building views is represented only by their size, maintenance and updates are not modelled, the data are static, and the bound is on benefit, not on query cost. On TPC-D data the greedy order reaches nearly the minimum total query time with five views and barely more space than the base view. | Read |
| [NOTE-898](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-898.md) | Finkelstein, Schkolnick & Tiberio — Physical database design for relational databases | DBDSGN chooses, for each table, one clustered (ordering) index and a set of nonclustered indices to minimise a frequency-weighted sum of per-statement costs (access, tuple update, index maintenance) plus a weighted storage term, under an optional page limit, taking every cost from the System R optimizer's own estimates rather than an external model. Statement costs for any configuration are computed exactly from "atomic" configurations with at most one index per table (Propositions 1 and 2), so the optimizer is consulted a linear rather than exponential number of times per table; with no elimination heuristics and a full search the tool finds the optimum, but only with respect to the optimizer's estimates. The paper gives one worked example and no measurement of actual execution, and its claims that the heuristics usually find the best solutions are not backed by reported data. | [NOTE-900](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-900.md) | Chaudhuri & Narasayya — An efficient, cost-driven index selection tool for Microsoft SQL Server | The AutoAdmin tool picks at most k indexes (single- or two-column, clustered or not) for a given workload of SQL statements, minimising the unweighted sum of the optimizer's estimated costs of those statements, with hypothetical ("what-if") indexes made visible to the optimizer by loading their statistics into the catalog. Its contribution is search efficiency: candidates are restricted to indexes in some single query's best configuration, enumeration is Greedy(m, k) (an exhaustive seed of m indexes, then greedy additions), costs of most configurations are derived from a few "atomic" ones, and two-column indexes are generated only from winning single columns. On five TPC-D workloads this cut running time to 10–24% of a baseline, with estimated-cost quality 0–7% worse, and Greedy(2, 4) matched the exhaustive optimum on four of five workloads and was within 1% on the fifth. | [NOTE-906](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-906.md) | Cho & Garcia-Molina — Synchronizing a database to improve freshness (SIGMOD 2000) | For a local copy of N items, each changing as an independent Poisson process with a known rate and refreshed at fixed intervals under a fixed total refresh rate, refreshing every item equally keeps the copy fresher and younger on average than refreshing in proportion to change rate, under any distribution of rates (proved in the technical report by convexity). The freshness-optimal allocation is neither: it rises and then falls with change rate, and gives no refresh at all to items that change too fast for the budget, while the age-optimal allocation rises slowly with change rate. On estimates from 270 web sites, proportional, uniform and optimal refresh give freshness 0.12, 0.57 and 0.62. Every item matters equally, staleness is a time average with no access or query model, the refresh budget is fixed rather than priced, and refresh, change and its detection are free of any other cost. | Read |
| [NOTE-908](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-908.md) | Labrinidis & Roussopoulos — WebView materialization | For a page built from database queries, the paper compares three ways to serve it on a server with online updates: compute it on each request (virt), store the query result in the DBMS and refresh it on every update (matdb), or store the finished page as a file at the web server and rewrite it on every update (matweb). It gives a cost model summing access and update costs by their frequencies and states the selection problem (choose a policy per page to minimize mean response time, no space limit, no staleness allowed), but gives no algorithm for it. On one Apache/Informix testbed with cheap indexed queries, matweb answered 10 to 230 times faster than the other two at all loads tried, and matdb was slower than virt whenever there were updates, because reading the stored result cost about as much as recomputing it. Staleness is defined as the delay from update to reply, sketched, and never measured; build cost and storage are outside the model. | Read |
| [NOTE-911](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-911.md) | Labrinidis & Roussopoulos — Balancing performance and data freshness in web database servers | The paper poses Online View Selection for a web server whose database takes updates while serving requests: choose, as the workload runs, which page fragments (WebViews) to keep stored and refreshed on every update and which to cache and invalidate, so as to minimize mean response time while the fraction of fresh fragments served (QoD) stays above a threshold θ. Its algorithm, OVIS(θ), estimates per fragment the response-time and QoD change of switching, and periodically switches up to MAX_CHANGE fragments greedily, spending a QoD surplus on speed or buying back a deficit; it materializes everything when it detects backlog. Nothing is proved: optimality of the greedy step is asserted, and the evidence is one synthetic simulation with fixed costs, in which OVIS kept QoD near θ, answered faster than caching alone, and recovered from overload. Upkeep and query savings share one cost, but staleness is a constraint set by the user, not a priced term, and build cost, switching cost and storage are absent. | Read |
| [NOTE-912](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-912.md) | Olston, Loo & Widom — Adaptive precision setting for cached approximate values | Olston, Loo and Widom set the width of each cached interval adaptively to minimize total refresh traffic. A narrow interval is escaped often (value-initiated refreshes, cost C_vr); a wide one is too imprecise for queries more often (query-initiated refreshes, cost C_qr). Under a model in which these probabilities go as 1/W² and W, the expected cost rate is least where ρ·P_vr = P_qr, ρ = 2C_vr/C_qr, and a rule that widens on value-initiated and narrows on query-initiated refreshes, with probabilities set by ρ, reached within 1% to 5% of the best fixed width in simulation. That the rule converges is argued, not proved. With exact copies required it matched an adaptive exact-caching algorithm, and where imprecision was allowed it beat it. Staleness is priced as refresh traffic only: there is no build cost, no cost of a wrong answer, and the interval is never wrong. | Read |
| [NOTE-922](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-922.md) | Olston & Widom — Offering a precision-performance tradeoff for aggregation queries over replicated data | Olston and Widom propose TRAPP: caches hold, for each numeric value, an interval its source guarantees to contain the current value, the source pushing a refresh whenever the value leaves it. A query carries a precision constraint R, and the system chooses which values to fetch exactly so that the answer interval is at most R wide whatever the true values, at least total refresh cost. For SUM (and AVG without a predicate) that choice is a 0/1 knapsack problem, NP-complete in general and polynomial with equal costs; COUNT and MIN have simple rules. Staleness becomes bounded imprecision, never error, and the cost of the source-side upkeep that guarantees this, and of setting the bound widths, is outside the optimization. The one experiment is 90 stock prices with random costs. | Read |
| [NOTE-928](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-928.md) | Linial, London & Rabinovich — the geometry of graphs | Every n-point metric embeds in ℓ₂ with distortion O(log n) in O(log n) dimensions (Theorem 3.2(1), attributed to Bourgain). Later extensions relax independence, one through a hypercube queue. | Read |
| [NOTE-1584](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1584.md) v2 | Gopalan et al. — The connectivity of Boolean satisfiability | Classifies, by the constraint language alone, how hard it is to tell whether two solutions of a Boolean CNF(S)-formula with constants are joined by single-variable flips through solutions. For tight languages st-connectivity is in P, connectivity in coNP and diameter linear; otherwise both are PSPACE-complete and diameter can be 2^Ω(√n). Tight properly contains Schaefer, and the boundary cuts across Boolean clones. Read in full, the hard side included. The boundary is slightly wrong as stated: the hard side stands, but Schwerdtfeger moves the easy side's boundary to "safely tight". | Read |
| [NOTE-1594](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1594.md) | Siemroth — Optimal budget rules against wasteful year-end spending | A two-year principal–agent model of year-end spending: the agent privately observes each year's need and gains α < 1 from spending above it. The principal commits to a roll-over share, audit rules and a punishment. Some roll-over is weakly better than none and works only if the share exceeds α; partial roll-over is optimal in a restricted region, full roll-over for most parameters. Audits are threshold rules, or an interval rule in year 1; punishment is maximal and never imposed; strategic underfunding can be optimal when audit and fund costs are high. | Read |
| [NOTE-1595](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1595.md) | Ito et al. — On the complexity of reconfiguration problems | Defines a reconfiguration problem as reachability between two feasible solutions through feasible solutions under a symmetric polynomial adjacency. Reconfiguration of any NP search problem is in PSPACE; for power supply, independent set, clique, vertex cover, set cover and 0–1 integer programming it is PSPACE-complete; for matroid bases and matchings it is in P. Optimising the worst intermediate objective is inapproximable for maxmin clique, strongly NP-hard for minmax power supply, and 2-approximable in linear time for minmax set cover. | Read |
| [NOTE-1597](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1597.md) | Kinoshita and Ohsaki — Bistable compliant frames converted from truss mechanisms | A bistable compliant truss mechanism, found by an earlier optimization, is converted into a single-piece frame by replacing each pin joint with a pseudo-joint of thin end regions and optimizing their area and length ratios (OPT2) to keep the output displacement and a second self-equilibrium state, under a strain cap that prevents a point hinge. In the one example the frame keeps the second equilibrium, with the largest thin-element strain at 0.99 of the cap. Computational, one example, no fabrication. | Read |
| [NOTE-1602](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1602.md) | Marsden and Zwart — Quantitative foundations for resource theories | Quantitative resource theories as categories enriched in a commutative quantale: the monoid combines the quantities of successive conversion steps (costs by +, connection strengths by min, probabilities by ×) and the join picks the best alternative. Free conversions are base Q-categories, costly ones Q-profunctors; a hierarchy of free constructions over lists of resources gives comonads for many-to-one conversions; every endomorphism generates a free internal monad, its reflexive–transitive closure. One quantale per theory; static resources; proofs sketched. | Read |
| [NOTE-1604](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1604.md) v2 | Chou, Chua, Teo and Zheng — Efficiency of the long chain and sparse structure | Analytical support for Jordan and Graves's chaining principle. Plants and products form a bipartite graph, and sales once demand is known are a max-flow. For balanced, identical systems with independent demand, the long chain keeps about 89.6% (uniform) and 96% (normal, CV 0.33) of full flexibility's expected sales as the system grows, but only 58% and about 70% of its gain over dedicated plants, and 75% of sales for two-point demand; in general a suitably sampled sparse structure comes within ε of full flexibility; with correlated demand a sparse structure can serve almost none of it. | Read |
| [NOTE-1611](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1611.md) | Eppstein — Computational complexities of folding | A survey with new results on what can be computed about folding. Flat-foldability of a finite crease pattern, NP-complete by earlier work, is fixed-parameter tractable in ply and treewidth, and the singly-exponential dependence on treewidth is optimal under ETH. Exact 3D folded shapes can need numbers outside radical and bounded-degree root computation. In "flaps and flips", squares hinged to a tabletop, reaching one flat state from another is PSPACE-complete and counting states #P-complete. Flat-foldability of self-similar patterns with infinitely many creases on a finite square is undecidable. | Read |
| [NOTE-1613](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1613.md) v2 | Schwerdtfeger — A computational trichotomy for connectivity of Boolean satisfiability | Shows, by examples and amended lemmas, that Gopalan et al.'s connectivity dichotomies for Boolean CSPs overlooked constraints with a repeated variable, which can destroy the component structure the easy side relies on, and restates their theorems with "safely tight" sets, closed under identification of variables. Proves the trichotomy they conjectured: connectivity in P for CPSS sets, coNP-complete for the other safely tight sets, PSPACE-complete otherwise. | Read |
| [NOTE-1618](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1618.md) v2 | Hua, Luo, Swersey and Wen — A geometrically convergent solution to spatial hypercube queueing models | Extends the exact hypercube queueing model to server-specific service rates, solved through a birth–death process and an equivalent reformulation that the authors state converges at a geometric rate under a technical bound on how far the rates differ (Assumption 3.1), and parallelizes it. The proof checks for equal rates and has a gap for unequal ones. Reported over 1,000 times faster than a sparse solver and over 500 times faster than simulation on EMS data; proofs and tables not checked here. Credits Larson (1974) with the model, the alternating hyperplane solution method and the TOUR algorithm. | Read |
| [NOTE-1620](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1620.md) v2 | Larson and Odoni — Urban Operations Research, the hypercube queueing model | The book's own statement of the hypercube queueing model, §5.4 read in full with its equations. N distinguishable units, each busy or free, over a city split into Poisson-source atoms, with a fixed preference list per atom; the state is a vertex of the N-cube, transitions run along its edges, and from the steady state come unit workloads, dispatch fractions by unit and atom, dispatches across response areas and travel times (a unit's own mean travel time only approximately). The three-server example re-derives exactly. The basic model evaluates response areas a user supplies; exact solution grows as 2^N, and Larson's approximation reduces it to N equations. | Read |
| [NOTE-1621](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1621.md) v2 | de Oliveira, de Sá and Martins — Multi-period bi-objective ambulance location in Belo Horizonte | Read in full. Multi-period forms of FLEET (deterministic) and of Sorensen and Church's LR-MEXCLP (expected coverage with area-specific busy fractions), with coverage by service type made independent, in which each ambulance's base is chosen period by period while bases, once open, stay open; a second objective, the number of bases, is traded against coverage by the ε-constraint method. Applied to Belo Horizonte's SAMU (427 nodes, 1,527 sites, 24 hourly periods, 7 ALS and 21 BLS). The abstract's relocation gains compare the 2019 bases with optimized ones; relocation alone adds at most 1.7 points. §2 surveys MEXCLP, MALP and LR-MEXCLP. | Read |
| [NOTE-1623](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1623.md) | Rockafellar and Uryasev — Optimization of conditional value-at-risk | The auxiliary function F_β(x, α) = α + (1−β)⁻¹ E[f(x, y) − α]⁺ is convex and continuously differentiable in α; its minimum is the β-CVaR and its leftmost minimizer the β-VaR, so CVaR is minimized over decisions by minimizing F_β jointly, a convex program for convex losses and a linear program for linear losses on sampled scenarios, with no normality assumed. Two small illustrations: a normal three-asset portfolio, where minimum CVaR, minimum VaR and minimum variance coincide, and a non-normal options hedge. Assumes a loss distribution without atoms. | Read |
| [NOTE-1740](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1740.md) | Davoudabadi, Makui and Rasouli — Introducing a predictive-oriented multi-stakeholder recommender system model | The authors propose a recommender that scores each candidate item for a user by combining (a) a user-side score and (b) an organization-side score. User side: a reference point built from the user's peak and most recent purchase utilities (peak-end rule), item distances to it split into gains and losses with a prospect-theory-style value function (the EXPTODIM method), and a "user flexibility" index from the diversity of the user's past purchases. Organization side: "organizational expectations" (target values on operational features such as workshop capacity), the similarity between the organization's projected state after an item is chosen and that target, and an "organizational flexibility" index from the Euclidean gap between current and ideal state. A weight adjustment function, bounded so neither side is ignored, gives more weight to the organization the more flexible the user is, and more to the user the more flexible the organization is. Evaluated by simulation only: a hypothetical manufacturer with 30 products (4 attributes), 3 workshops with capacity limits, and 100 synthetic users; compared with a "customer-driven" strategy, it reduces over- and under-use of workshop capacity, reported as a 17.6% average improvement in capacity utilization. | Read |
| [NOTE-1778](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1778.md) | Gan (2022) — Gacha Game: When Prospect Theory Meets Optimal Pricing | A seller sells one good to a buyer with cumulative prospect theory preferences whose value is known. Probability weighting makes the buyer dynamically inconsistent. If she is naive, the unique optimum is a stationary loot box (a constant chance of the good per paid period); if sophisticated, the optimum adds worst-case insurance: after enough failures she can buy the good outright, which resembles the "pity system" of gacha games. With payments restricted to be non-negative (no paying the buyer), profit is bounded; with negative prices allowed, as in gambling, it is not, which Gan offers as a theoretical line between loot boxes and gambling and a reason to watch resale markets. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1885](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1885.md) | Moerman, Schraagen, Braaksma and van Dongen — Graceful extensibility in asset management: extending the capacity to adapt in managing cyber-physical railway systems | The authors code 430 items from reports on the failed Fyra V250 high-speed train introduction (Netherlands–Belgium, services cancelled after two months) and match them against 24 sub-patterns of Woods's ten proto-theorems by pattern-matching analysis. Most patterns are observed; some are not (the CfM concept itself was not recognised in the case; base vs extended adaptive capacity (S7) was not recognised). They propose operational guidelines and argue that asset management should accept indeterminism alongside deterministic planning. | Skimmed |
